acts.title: Text A · The photograph that is not a photograph
text: Two people are sitting in what looks like a small orange rubber boat, holding a single wooden paddle between them. It appears that the boat is being swept down a wild river and is about to drop over a waterfall.

At the bottom, waiting, is an enormous grey crocodile. It is half-submerged, so that only the top of its head is visible, but its eyes are bright orange and distinctly threatening. The woman in the boat is waving both hands in the air. Both of them are screaming.

None of it happened. The image is three separate photographs, and the crocodile was asleep in a zoo in Florida when it was taken. What makes it convincing is not the joins, which are visible if you look, but the light: somebody matched the shadows, and the eye accepts almost anything once the shadows agree.

items.q: What does the text reveal about the image?
o: It is three photographs combined, and none of it happened
It is a famous news photograph

items.q: What makes the image convincing, according to the writer?

acts.title: Text B · Why the eye is so easy to fool
text: The second image shows a man crouching against a low concrete wall, apparently on a narrow ledge near the top of a tall burning building. Below him, two uniformed police officers are looking up and seem to be shouting. Two figures in long black leather capes are climbing a rope towards him.

Almost everybody who sees it laughs before they think, and that order matters. Vision is not a recording. The brain receives a poor, upside-down, low-detail signal and constructs a scene from it, using what it expects to be there.

That is why the crocodile works and why the capes do not. A grey shape in dark water is what the brain expects; a superhero on a rope is not. The illusion fails not because the image is worse but because the expectation is missing.
What we call seeing is mostly prediction, corrected by light.

acts.title: The order nobody was taught and everybody follows
rule: English puts adjectives in a fixed order before a noun. Native speakers cannot state the rule and never break it: a green big dragon sounds wrong to them without their knowing why. The order runs from opinion, which is furthest from the noun, to the material it is made of, which is closest.
points: opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose → NOUN.
OSASCOMP. You will only ever need three or four of them at once.
An opinion adjective — beautiful, horrible, lovely — always goes in front of any fact adjective.
Adjectives of the same type take a comma: a cold, wet morning. Different types do not: a small orange rubber boat.
More than three before a noun reads as a list, and a good writer breaks it up.
eg: Two of the same type — comma.
A modifier plus a colour: bright belongs with orange.
size, then the -ing form describing the state.
acts.careful: Opinion goes furthest from the noun, not nearest. “a plastic horrible chair” is wrong; “a horrible plastic chair” is right, because horrible is what you think and plastic is what it is.

acts.title: Four adjectives, one noun, in order
steps: Four words. Only one order works.
1 · The noun goes last. Everything else is queuing in front of it.
2 · MATERIAL sits closest to the noun. Always.
3 · COLOUR goes in front of material.
4 · SIZE goes in front of colour. If there were an opinion, it would go in front of everything.

write.q: Describe a photograph in about 180 words — one on your wall, on your phone, or in the news. Keep what you can see separate from what you infer. Use at least four noun phrases with two or more adjectives in front of them, in the correct order, and at least three inference phrases.
write.model:
In the foreground there is a young woman in a long grey woollen coat, standing at the edge of a frozen lake with her back to the camera. She is holding what looks like a thermos flask.

Behind her the ice runs to a low wooded shore, and about halfway across there are two small dark figures who appear to be walking rather than skating. A pale winter sun sits just above the trees.

It looks as if it is very early, partly because of the light and partly because there are no other tracks on the snow except one set leading to where she stands.

It appears that she is waiting rather than resting. She is not sitting down, the flask is unopened, and she is facing the two figures rather than the shore.

What I cannot tell is whether she knows them. That is the whole reason I kept the photograph, and it is the one thing the image refuses to say.
